name: wren
desc: Small, fast, class-based concurrent scripting language
why: A small, clean, class-based scripting language with fibers, a lesser-known and pleasantly unusual embeddable language.

brief.what_it_is: Wren is a small, class-based scripting language with lightweight fibers for concurrency, meant to be embedded in host applications. Its README describes it as a small, fast, class-based concurrent scripting language. It takes Wren source code, such as a script that prints a greeting, defines a class, or steps through a fiber, and runs it on its own bytecode VM. The README says the VM implementation is under 4,000 semicolons. It has no dependencies and a small standard library, and it exposes a C API for embedding.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames Wren as Smalltalk in a Lua-sized package with a dash of Erlang, wrapped in familiar modern syntax. Its stated goal is a scripting language that puts classes front and center, since the author says many scripting languages have unusual or non-existent object models.
brief.how_it_works: A fast single-pass compiler turns source into tight bytecode, and a compact object representation helps performance, according to the README. Concurrency comes from lightweight fibers that are core to the execution model, letting a program be organized as communicating coroutines. Fibers are created with Fiber.new, run with call, and produce values with Fiber.yield.
brief.install_notes: The README says Wren has no dependencies and compiles cleanly as C99, C++98 or anything later, which suggests building from source with a C compiler, but the README does not give build steps. Embedding goes through the C API. The getting-started page at wren.io/getting-started.html is linked from the README but was not fetched, so first-run steps are unverified. There is also a browser playground linked from the README that can be tried without installing anything.
brief.standout: Fibers as the core concurrency primitive in a tiny embeddable language are unusual, and the author's stated 'army of communicating coroutines' framing makes that concrete. The project also puts real effort into readability: the README says the VM is small but not dense and is lovingly commented.
brief.status: unknown. The README does not give a release version or date, and I did not see a last commit date or changelog. The README's build badge points to travis-ci.org, which suggests the CI setup may be old, but that is not proof the project is inactive. A release or commit page would settle it.
brief.caveats: The brew entry lists no executables, so the Homebrew install may not provide a wren command-line binary. I could not confirm that from the pages. The getting-started and docs pages were not read. No licence was seen in the fetched pages. The CI badge links to travis-ci.org. The README does not discuss platform support beyond the C standard requirement.
quotes: Think Smalltalk in a Lua-sized package with a dash of Erlang and wrapped up in a familiar, modern syntax.
Wren is small. The VM implementation is under 4,000 semicolons.
Lightweight fibers are core to the execution model and let you organize your program into an army of communicating coroutines.
